passage: Sagar kept a magazine picture of the game console folded in his pocket: two thousand rupees. Dad had already said it was too much this month. Sagar could sulk, but he sat on the roof steps in Kathmandu and made himself think. If I insist, I may get nothing. A cheaper one still plays games. Or I wait until my birthday in two months, and Dad might say yes then. That night he said, "Dad, could I have the smaller console, or wait till my birthday and put my own savings towards it?" Dad rubbed his chin. "That I can think about." Sagar decided that half a loaf was better than none.

qa.q: How much did the console in Sagar's picture cost?
qa.a: The console cost two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Sagar feeling as he sat on the roof steps, and what did he decide to do about it?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and tempted to sulk, but he chose to think through his options instead.

qa.q: What else could Sagar do to make a compromise more likely?
qa.a: He could offer his own savings or take on extra chores, because it shows effort and lowers what Dad has to pay.

qa.q: How might Dad feel hearing two options instead of a flat demand?
qa.a: Probably relieved and more willing to talk, since he said he could think about it.

grounding: A boy wanting an expensive console accepts that a cheaper one or waiting for his birthday is better than nothing.

passage: During the free period in the school library, Sahil opened his notebook to the page where he'd written CONSOLE, 2000 RUPEES in big letters. His friend Disha peered over. "Your parents said no?" "They said not now. Too much." Sahil tapped his pen. "So I've been thinking. Option one: keep asking and get nothing. Option two: the small handheld one, eight hundred, with old games built in. Option three: wait till my birthday in March, when Nani usually gives a gift." "Which one?" "The handheld has fewer games. March is five months away." He drew a line under option two. "I'd rather have some fun now than none. I can still hope for the big one later." That evening he asked his parents about the handheld, and they said they'd look at it with him on Saturday.

qa.q: What did Sahil write in big letters?
How did Sahil feel choosing the handheld?
qa.a: A little disappointed not to get the big one, but content and relieved to have a realistic choice.

qa.q: What else could Sahil have considered?
qa.a: Waiting for March and talking it over with his parents then, since a birthday gift might change what is possible.

qa.q: How might Sahil's parents see his new request?
qa.a: They seem pleased by the reasonable compromise, agreeing to look at the handheld with him on Saturday.

grounding: A boy accepts that a cheaper option or waiting for his birthday could work, choosing part of what he wants over nothing.

passage: I'm Mridul, Saurabh's cousin. We were at the electronics shop on Sunday, and Saurabh stood in front of the game console for a long time. Two thousand rupees. His father said, "That's a lot for now." I thought Saurabh would sulk. Instead he walked along the shelf, picking things up: a cheaper console with fewer games, a pair of controllers for the old game box at home. Then he came back and said, "Papa, if I get the controllers now, can we think about the console for my birthday?" His father smiled. "That sounds fair." In the car Saurabh was quiet but not sulky. I don't know if he was disappointed. He kept turning the controller box over in his hands.

qa.q: How much did the console cost?
What might Saurabh have felt in the car?
qa.a: Perhaps a little disappointed, but also content with getting part of what he wanted.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh have suggested?
qa.a: The cheaper console with fewer games, which would give him a new console now instead of waiting.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Saurabh's choice?
qa.a: Mridul expected sulking and is surprised by the compromise, but cannot tell whether Saurabh was disappointed.

grounding: A cousin watches a boy accept a smaller purchase now and the console perhaps on his birthday, instead of nothing.
